hops.title: Cold War bomb tests birthdated human cortical neurons
hops.text: Nobody can give a human baby a pulse of radioactive thymidine to find out when its cortical neurons are born. The Cold War ran a version of that experiment on everyone. Above-ground nuclear tests sent atmospheric carbon-14 soaring, and after 1963 it fell steeply enough to date cells. Carbon from food is built into newly made DNA, and a cell that never divides again keeps that record. In 2005 and 2006, Kirsty Spalding, Ratan Bhardwaj and Jonas Frisen measured carbon-14 in adult human brain DNA. Non-neuronal cells had turned over; neocortical neurons dated to around the person's own birth, with no detectable replacement later.

sources.citation: Spalding KL et al., Retrospective birth dating of cells in humans, Cell 122(1):133-143 (2005), PMID 16009139
Bhardwaj RD et al., Neocortical neurogenesis in humans is restricted to development, PNAS 103(33):12564-12568 (2006), PMID 16901981

image.caption: Bomb-test carbon-14 dated neocortical neurons to around birth, with no detectable replacement in adulthood.

hops.afterHeading: Needed, but what does it say?
hops.title: Turn a houseplant and move its light
hops.text: A leafy plant on a sunny windowsill leans toward the glass. Turn the pot so the stems point into the room, then watch the growing tips over the following days for a new bend toward the window. Blue-light photoreceptors in the plant read the direction the light comes from and shift the hormone auxin to the shaded flank, which grows faster, so the stem curves. Same window, same light, arriving at the shoots from the other side. The Reelin experiments in this section ask a related question: what happens when neurons get the signal from a different place, or in a different pattern?

sources.citation: Sakai T, Haga K, Molecular genetic analysis of phototropism in Arabidopsis, Plant Cell Physiol. 53(9):1517-1534 (2012), PMCID PMC3439871

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: Hands turning a terracotta pot holding a leaning leafy plant on a sunny windowsill so its curved stems point into the room.
image.caption: Turn the pot and the plant keeps its light, but the window now reaches the shoots from the other side.

hops.title: A rare Reelin variant in an unusually resilient Alzheimer's carrier
hops.text: In Colombia's largest known family with hereditary early-onset Alzheimer's, carriers of a presenilin-1 mutation reach mild cognitive impairment at a median age of 44 and dementia at 49. One carrier worked into his early sixties. His first cognitive assessment at 67 found subtle difficulties, doctors diagnosed mild cognitive impairment at 70, and scans at 73 showed heavy amyloid. In 2023 researchers reported he carried one copy of a rare Reelin variant, COLBOS, and had lower entorhinal tau burden than typical carriers. Its mouse equivalent raised Dab1 phosphorylation in cultured mouse cortical neurons and in the cerebellum and hippocampus of homozygous male mice. One man is a lead, not a proof.

sources.citation: Lopera F et al., Resilience to autosomal dominant Alzheimer's disease in a Reelin-COLBOS heterozygous man, Nat. Med. 29(5):1243-1252 (2023), PMCID PMC10202812
Lopera F et al., Resilience to autosomal dominant Alzheimer's disease in a Reelin-COLBOS heterozygous man, Nat. Med. 29(5):1243-1252 (2023), PMID 37188781
